topics.title: Historical Era of India
pointers: Origin: Introduced by Scottish historian James Mill in his book The History of British India (1817). He divided Indian history purely on the basis of the religion of the rulers:
Hindu Period (Ancient): Portrayed as an era of Hindu rulers (up to the arrival of Muslim invaders).

Muslim Period (Medieval – from c. 712 AD / 1206 AD): Marked from the Arab invasion of Sindh by Muhammad bin Qasim (712 AD) or the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate (1206 AD), portrayed as an era of Muslim rule.
British / Christian Period (Modern – from 1757 AD): Marked from the Battle of Plassey (1757 AD), portrayed as a period of British/Christian rule bringing modern civilization.

Critique: Modern historians rejected this classification because it was communal, Eurocentric, and historically inaccurate (ignoring that rulers of different faiths coexisted in every era and overlooking deeper social, economic, and cultural changes).

(Note: Standard NCERT/R.S. Sharma timelines span from Prehistory / 1500 BC [Vedic Age] up to c. 750 AD [Early Medieval transition], while broader classifications extend Ancient India up to c. 1200 AD [establishment of the Delhi Sultanate].)

Context: In recent years (especially post-2014), there has been renewed debate and revision in Indian historiography and school textbooks (NCERT) to incorporate indigenous perspectives, cultural continuity, and new archaeological findings.

topics.fullNotes:
1. Colonial / Communal Periodization (James Mill, 1817)

Origin: Introduced by Scottish historian James Mill in his book The History of British India (1817). He divided Indian history purely on the basis of the religion of the rulers:

Hindu Period (Ancient): Portrayed as an era of Hindu rulers (up to the arrival of Muslim invaders).

Muslim Period (Medieval – from c. 712 AD / 1206 AD): Marked from the Arab invasion of Sindh by Muhammad bin Qasim (712 AD) or the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate (1206 AD), portrayed as an era of Muslim rule.

British / Christian Period (Modern – from 1757 AD): Marked from the Battle of Plassey (1757 AD), portrayed as a period of British/Christian rule bringing modern civilization.

Critique: Modern historians rejected this classification because it was communal, Eurocentric, and historically inaccurate (ignoring that rulers of different faiths coexisted in every era and overlooking deeper social, economic, and cultural changes).

2. Modern / Secular Periodization (Based on Socio-Economic & Political Transitions)

Ancient India (Earliest times / Prehistory up to c. 750 AD or 1200 AD):

(Note: Standard NCERT/R.S. Sharma timelines span from Prehistory / 1500 BC [Vedic Age] up to c. 750 AD [Early Medieval transition], while broader classifications extend Ancient India up to c. 1200 AD [establishment of the Delhi Sultanate].)

Medieval India (c. 750 AD / 1200 AD – 1757 AD):

Divided into Early Medieval (c. 750–1200 AD, marked by regional kingdoms and feudalism) and Late Medieval (c. 1200–1757 AD, Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire), ending with the Battle of Plassey (1757 AD).

Modern India (1757 AD onwards):

Marked by the rise of British colonial rule, socio-religious reform movements, the Indian National Movement, and Independence (1947).

3. Contemporary Historiographical Shifts (Post-2014)

Context: In recent years (especially post-2014), there has been renewed debate and revision in Indian historiography and school textbooks (NCERT) to incorporate indigenous perspectives, cultural continuity, and new archaeological findings.

Key Figure – Meenakshi Jain: A prominent contemporary Indian historian (former professor at Gargi College, University of Delhi, and Padma Shri awardee) known for her works on ancient and medieval Indian history, cultural heritage, and textbook revisions (such as Medieval India for NCERT and books on Rama, Ayodhya, and temple history).

topics.title: Chronological Timeline: Prehistory
pointers: Meaning: Old Stone Age (Pleistocene period).

Key Features: People were hunter-gatherers and food gatherers with no knowledge of agriculture or pottery; used crude, unpolished stone tools (hand axes, cleavers, choppers, and scrapers made mainly of quartzite).
Meaning: Middle Stone Age (transitional phase between Palaeolithic and Neolithic).
Key Features: Domestication of animals began (the dog was the first domesticated animal, followed by sheep and goats).

Tools: Characterized by Microliths—tiny, sharp, geometric stone tools (typically 1–5 cm in length, made of chert, jasper, or chalcedony). (Note: Polished stone tools are a hallmark of the Neolithic age, not Mesolithic.)
Earliest Evidence of Domestication in India: Adamgarh (Madhya Pradesh) and Bagor (Rajasthan), dating to around 5000 BC.
Key Features: Beginning of agriculture (wheat, barley, rice), pottery (first handmade, later wheel-made), polished stone tools (celts), and settled village life.
Earliest Agricultural Settlement: Mehrgarh (in Balochistan, Pakistan), dating back to c. 7000 BC.
topics.fullNotes:
Palaeolithic Age (c. 2,00,000 BC – 10,000 BC | or up to 5,00,000 BC in the Indian context):

Meaning: Old Stone Age (Pleistocene period).

Key Features: People were hunter-gatherers and food gatherers with no knowledge of agriculture or pottery; used crude, unpolished stone tools (hand axes, cleavers, choppers, and scrapers made mainly of quartzite).

Mesolithic Age (c. 10,000 BC – 8,000 BC / 6,000 BC):

Meaning: Middle Stone Age (transitional phase between Palaeolithic and Neolithic).

Key Features: Domestication of animals began (the dog was the first domesticated animal, followed by sheep and goats).

Tools: Characterized by Microliths—tiny, sharp, geometric stone tools (typically 1–5 cm in length, made of chert, jasper, or chalcedony). (Note: Polished stone tools are a hallmark of the Neolithic age, not Mesolithic.)

Earliest Evidence of Domestication in India: Adamgarh (Madhya Pradesh) and Bagor (Rajasthan), dating to around 5000 BC.

Neolithic Age (c. 8,000 BC / 7,000 BC – 4,000 BC / 1,000 BC):

Meaning: New Stone Age.

Key Features: Beginning of agriculture (wheat, barley, rice), pottery (first handmade, later wheel-made), polished stone tools (celts), and settled village life.

Earliest Agricultural Settlement: Mehrgarh (in Balochistan, Pakistan), dating back to c. 7000 BC.

Chalcolithic Age (c. 4,000 BC – 1,500 BC / 700 BC):

Meaning: Copper-Stone Age (first use of metal—copper—alongside stone tools).

Key Features: Predominantly rural settlements (unable to support large cities like the Bronze Age Harappans), subsistence farming, and distinctive Black-and-Red Ware (BRW) pottery.

topics.fullNotes:
Indus Valley Civilization / Harappan Civilization (c. 2700 BC – 1800 BC | Mature Phase: c. 2600 – 1900 BC):

Classification: Proto-history (a script existed, namely the pictographic Harappan script, though it remains undeciphered) and a Bronze Age society.

Key Features: First urbanization in India, renowned for advanced urban planning (grid-pattern streets, burnt-brick houses, and covered drainage systems), extensive trade (internal and external with Mesopotamia), and distinctive steatite seals.

Vedic Age (c. 1500 BC – 600 BC):

Phases: Divided into the Early Vedic / Rigvedic Period (c. 1500–1000 BC) and the Later Vedic Period (c. 1000–600 BC).

Key Features: Indo-Aryan migration/settlement, composition and compilation of the Vedas and Vedic literature, and the use of iron (around 1000 BC in the Later Vedic phase, referred to as Shyama/Krishna Ayas), which cleared dense Gangetic forests and transformed agriculture.

Age of Mahajanapadas (c. 6th Century BC / 600 BC):

Key Features: Marked the second urbanization in Indian history (centered in the Gangetic plains), the emergence of 16 Great States (Mahajanapadas)—both monarchies and republics (Ganasanghas)—the rise of Magadha as the dominant empire, and the birth of heterodox religious movements, notably Buddhism and Jainism.

topics.fullNotes:
Mauryan Empire (c. 321 – 185 BC):

Key Rulers: Chandragupta Maurya, Bindusara, and Ashoka.

Key Features: First pan-Indian empire with a centralized administration; famous for Ashokan Pillars and rock edicts propagating Dhamma.

Post-Mauryan Period (c. 200 BC – 300 AD):

Key Features: Political disintegration of the Mauryan Empire, followed by foreign invasions from the northwest (Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians, and Kushanas) and the rise of indigenous powers like the Satavahanas in the Deccan.

Economy: Flourishing internal and external trade (especially with the Roman Empire) and extensive coinage (gold and copper coins of the Kushanas; lead, potin, and copper coins of the Satavahanas).

Gupta Empire (c. 300 AD – 550/600 AD – "Golden Age"):

Key Features: Often termed the "Golden Age" (or Classical Age) of ancient India due to remarkable achievements in classical Sanskrit literature (Kalidasa), the beginnings of structural temple architecture (Nagara style), art (Sarnath school of sculpture, Ajanta paintings), and science & mathematics (Aryabhata, Varahamihira).

Post-Gupta Period (c. 600 AD onwards):

Key Features: Political disintegration after the fall of the Guptas, the rise of regional kingdoms (such as the Pushyabhutis under Harshavardhana in the north, Chalukyas in the Deccan, and Pallavas in the south), and feudal beginnings (widespread land grants to officials and Brahmans, decline of trade, and ruralization of the economy).

topics.fullNotes:
1. Historiography

Definition: The study of the methods, sources, and perspectives used in the construction/writing of history

.

2. Development of a Composite Culture

Fusion of Ethnic Groups: Ancient India witnessed the continuous arrival and assimilation of diverse ethnic groups—including Pre-Aryans, Indo-Aryans, Greeks (Indo-Greeks), Scythians (Shakas), Hunas, and Turks—each contributing to the making of Indian culture.

Cultural & Linguistic Interaction:

Deep interaction occurred between Pre-Aryan cultures and incoming Aryan traditions.

Dravidian and Tamil cultures in the south interacted closely with northern Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Pali traditions.

Many Munda and Dravidian terms were absorbed into Vedic Sanskrit, while northern ideas entered early Tamil Sangam literature.

Religion: Ancient India served as the birthplace of major world religions—Hinduism (Brahmanism), Jainism, and Buddhism—which coexisted and influenced one another over centuries.

3. Unity, Geography, and the Name of the Country

Name of the Country: Known as Bharatavarsha (the land of the Bharatas, an ancient Rigvedic tribe), and its people were called Bharatasamtati (descendants of Bharata).

Geographical Vision: Ancient poets, philosophers, and rulers viewed the entire subcontinent stretching from the Himalayas to the sea as a single cultural and geographical unit. Kings who strove to establish authority over this entire landmass were celebrated as Chakravartins (universal monarchs).

Names Given by Foreigners:

India: Derived by the Greeks from the river Sindhu (which became Indos in Greek).

Hind / Hindustan: Derived from the river Sindhu by the Iranians/Persians (who pronounced 'S' as 'H', turning Sindhu into Hindu), and later popularized as Hindustan by Persian and Arabic writers/travellers.

Lingua Francas (Unifying Languages):

Prakrit served as the common lingua franca across much of India in the 3rd century BC (used in Ashoka’s inscriptions), alongside Pali (used in early Buddhist texts).

Sanskrit later emerged as the dominant pan-Indian language of administration, literature, and culture from the Gupta period (4th century AD) onward.

topics.title: Modern Historians of Ancient India
pointers: Core Motivation: Modern research into ancient India began in the second half of the 18th century to serve the administrative needs of British colonial rule (specifically to understand local laws, customs, and revenue systems).

Warren Hastings (First Governor-General of Bengal): Established the Calcutta Madrasa in 1781 (for the study of Muslim law and related subjects; later, Jonathan Duncan established the Sanskrit College at Banaras in 1791 for Hindu law)

Commissioned the translation of the Manusmriti into English in 1776 under the title A Code of Gentoo Laws (compiled by Hindu pundits in Sanskrit, translated into Persian, and then rendered into English by Nathaniel Brassey Halhed)
Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784): Founded in Calcutta in 1784 by Sir William Jones
Jones translated Kalidasa’s famous play Abhijnanashakuntalam into English in 1789 and highlighted the close linguistic affinity between Sanskrit and European languages (Indo-European family)
Charles Wilkins (1785): Translated the Bhagavad Gita into English in 1785 (with a foreword by Warren Hastings)
topics.fullNotes:
Early Colonial & Orientalist Research (Second Half of the 18th Century)

Core Motivation: Modern research into ancient India began in the second half of the 18th century to serve the administrative needs of British colonial rule (specifically to understand local laws, customs, and revenue systems).

Warren Hastings (First Governor-General of Bengal):

Established the Calcutta Madrasa in 1781 (for the study of Muslim law and related subjects; later, Jonathan Duncan established the Sanskrit College at Banaras in 1791 for Hindu law).

Commissioned the translation of the Manusmriti into English in 1776 under the title A Code of Gentoo Laws (compiled by Hindu pundits in Sanskrit, translated into Persian, and then rendered into English by Nathaniel Brassey Halhed).

Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784):

Founded in Calcutta in 1784 by Sir William Jones.

Jones translated Kalidasa’s famous play Abhijnanashakuntalam into English in 1789 and highlighted the close linguistic affinity between Sanskrit and European languages (Indo-European family).

Charles Wilkins (1785):

Translated the Bhagavad Gita into English in 1785 (with a foreword by Warren Hastings).

Expansion of Asiatic Societies:

Bombay Asiatic Society (originally the Literary Society of Bombay) was founded in 1804 by Sir James Mackintosh.

Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland was set up in London in 1823.

Impact of the Revolt of 1857 & Christian Missionaries:

The Revolt of 1857 made the British realize they needed a deeper knowledge of Indian society, manners, and customs to prevent future uprisings and govern effectively.

Christian Missionaries studied Indian religions and texts primarily to point out weaknesses in Hindu society, win conversions to Christianity, and thereby strengthen the British Empire.

Max Müller (Editor):

Most ancient Indian scriptures were translated into English under the general editorship of German-born Indologist F. Max Müller, published in the massive 50-volume series The Sacred Books of the East (starting in 1879).

topics.title: General observations by colonial historians  for India history
pointers: Lack of Historical Sense: Claimed ancient Indians lacked a proper sense of history, particularly regarding time and chronology.
Oriental Despotism: Asserted that Indians were accustomed to despotic rule and had no tradition of self-government or democratic institutions.
Excessive Spiritualism: Portrayed Indian history as purely spiritual and other-worldly, ignoring material, economic, and scientific developments.
Static Social Structure: Highlighted the caste system and social discrimination as proof that Indian society was rigid, stagnant, and incapable of progress.
Absence of Nationalism: Argued that Indians lacked any feeling of nationalism or political unity until the arrival of British rule.
Objective: Used these generalizations to denigrate Indian character and achievements, thereby providing ideological justification for British colonial rule.
topics.fullNotes:
Colonial / Imperialist Approach to Ancient Indian History

Key Assumptions of Colonial Historians:

Lack of Historical Sense: Claimed ancient Indians lacked a proper sense of history, particularly regarding time and chronology.

Oriental Despotism: Asserted that Indians were accustomed to despotic rule and had no tradition of self-government or democratic institutions.

Excessive Spiritualism: Portrayed Indian history as purely spiritual and other-worldly, ignoring material, economic, and scientific developments.

Static Social Structure: Highlighted the caste system and social discrimination as proof that Indian society was rigid, stagnant, and incapable of progress.

Absence of Nationalism: Argued that Indians lacked any feeling of nationalism or political unity until the arrival of British rule.

Key Representative – Vincent Arthur Smith (1843–1920):

Wrote Early History of India (1904), the first systematic history of ancient India.

Gave primacy to political history and exaggerated the role of foreign invasions (e.g., devoting nearly one-third of his book solely to Alexander’s invasion).

Concluded that Indians were incapable of governing themselves without a strong foreign power (like the British) to maintain order.

Objective: Used these generalizations to denigrate Indian character and achievements, thereby providing ideological justification for British colonial rule.

topics.title: Nationalist approach and contribution
pointers: Key Figures: Raja Rammohan Roy, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Dadabhai Naoroji, Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, Lala Lajpat Rai, and Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
Rajendralal Mitra: Published several Vedic texts and wrote Indo-Aryans, proving that ancient Indian society was rational and progressive (even noting practices like beef-eating in ancient times).

Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar & Vishwanath Kashinath Rajwade: Dedicated their lives to reconstructing India’s social and political history using primary sources (Bhandarkar reconstructed the political history of the Deccan/Satavahanas and the history of Vaishnavism; Rajwade compiled 22 volumes of Maratha histor...
Pandurang Vaman Kane: Wrote the monumental History of Dharmashastra (in five volumes), which serves as an encyclopedia of ancient social laws, customs, and social processes.
Devadatta Ramakrishna Bhandarkar: Wrote extensively on Ashoka and ancient Indian political institutions, using epigraphic evidence.

Hemchandra Raychaudhuri: Reconstructed the political history of ancient India from the time of the Mahabharata War (c. 10th century BC) to the end of the Gupta Empire (Political History of Ancient India).
R.C. Majumdar: General editor of the multi-volume publication The History and Culture of the Indian People, highlighting the achievements of Indian civilization.
K.A. Nilakanta Sastri: Pioneered the reconstruction of the history of South India (A History of South India), emphasizing cultural harmony and Chola administration.
topics.fullNotes:
1. Early Social Reformers & Nationalist Thinkers

Context:

Reconstructed ancient Indian history to counter colonial narratives, promote social reform, and build a case for self-government (Swaraj).

Key Figures: Raja Rammohan Roy, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Dadabhai Naoroji, Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, Lala Lajpat Rai, and Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

2. Key Nationalist Historians & Their Contributions

Rajendralal Mitra: Published several Vedic texts and wrote Indo-Aryans, proving that ancient Indian society was rational and progressive (even noting practices like beef-eating in ancient times).

Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar & Vishwanath Kashinath Rajwade: Dedicated their lives to reconstructing India’s social and political history using primary sources (Bhandarkar reconstructed the political history of the Deccan/Satavahanas and the history of Vaishnavism; Rajwade compiled 22 volumes of Maratha history).

Pandurang Vaman Kane: Wrote the monumental History of Dharmashastra (in five volumes), which serves as an encyclopedia of ancient social laws, customs, and social processes.

Devadatta Ramakrishna Bhandarkar: Wrote extensively on Ashoka and ancient Indian political institutions, using epigraphic evidence.

Hemchandra Raychaudhuri: Reconstructed the political history of ancient India from the time of the Mahabharata War (c. 10th century BC) to the end of the Gupta Empire (Political History of Ancient India).

R.C. Majumdar: General editor of the multi-volume publication The History and Culture of the Indian People, highlighting the achievements of Indian civilization.

K.A. Nilakanta Sastri: Pioneered the reconstruction of the history of South India (A History of South India), emphasizing cultural harmony and Chola administration.

K.P. Jayaswal: Wrote Hindu Polity (1924), in which he exploded the colonial myth of Indian despotism, demonstrating that ancient India had republics (Ganasanghas) and constitutional monarchies.

topics.fullNotes:
Nationalist Historians' Counter-Arguments (Response to Vincent Smith & Colonial Views)

India Had a Rich Political History: Countered the colonial claim that India lacked political unity or historical sense by proving that ancient India had vast empires (such as the Mauryas and Guptas) and strong political traditions.

Expertise in Administration: Highlighted indigenous texts like Kautilya’s Arthashastra and inscriptions to show that Indians possessed advanced expertise in administration, statecraft, and local self-government (such as Ganasanghas/republics and Chola village assemblies).

Less Space to Alexander’s Invasion: Corrected Vincent Smith’s exaggeration (where he gave nearly one-third of his book to Alexander) by giving far less space to Alexander’s invasion, treating it as a minor military raid in northwestern India that left no lasting political impact.

Dialogue of Porus: Highlighted the famous episode where King Porus boldly demanded to be treated "as a king would treat another king" after his defeat by Alexander—using it to showcase Indian courage, dignity, and resistance against foreign invaders.

Limitation (Overplayed the Indigenous Role): In their zeal to counter colonial bias and glorify the past, some nationalist historians overplayed the role of indigenous elements, often ignoring or minimizing genuine cultural and institutional contributions brought by foreign contacts (such as the Indo-Greeks, Shakas, and Kushanas).

British Historian – A.L. Basham: Wrote The Wonder That Was India (1954). Unlike earlier colonial historians who focused heavily on political conquests and despotism, he highlighted India's rich cultural, social, and religious heritage.

Indian Historian – D.D. Kosambi: Wrote An Introduction to the Study of Indian History (1956). He pioneered a Marxist/materialist approach, shifting the focus from dynastic history to socio-economic foundations and technological changes.

New Historians (Post-1950s/60s Trends):

Shifted emphasis toward social, economic, and cultural processes and tried to relate them to political developments.

Analyzed the stratification of society (caste and class) and agrarian expansion.

Did not magnify the role of religion (earlier colonial/traditional historians magnified religion and spiritualism; modern historians contextualized religion within material and social developments rather than treating it as the sole driving force).

topics.title: Nature of sources and Historical Construction
pointers: Prehistoric Age: No written sources exist; history is reconstructed through material remains buried in mounds.
Types of Mounds: Single-culture, major-culture, and multi-culture mounds.
Excavation: Conducted either vertically or horizontally (lengthwise/widespread digging to get a complete picture of a site).
Study: Known as numismatics; helps reconstruct political, economic, and cultural history.

Post-Vedic (5th Century BC): Punch-marked silver coins appeared, known as Karshapana or Shatamana.

Indo-Greeks (c. 2nd Century BC / 180 BC): First rulers in India to issue coins that can be definitively attributed to specific kings (featuring the king's portrait and name), and the first to issue gold coins in India.

topics.fullNotes:
1. Material Remains

Prehistoric Age: No written sources exist; history is reconstructed through material remains buried in mounds.

Types of Mounds: Single-culture, major-culture, and multi-culture mounds.

Excavation: Conducted either vertically or horizontally (lengthwise/widespread digging to get a complete picture of a site).

2. Coins

Study: Known as numismatics; helps reconstruct political, economic, and cultural history.

Vedic Period: Nishka is mentioned in the Vedas (used as a gold ornament/unit of value, though no actual coins from this era have been found).

Post-Vedic (5th Century BC): Punch-marked silver coins appeared, known as Karshapana or Shatamana.

Indo-Greeks (c. 2nd Century BC / 180 BC): First rulers in India to issue coins that can be definitively attributed to specific kings (featuring the king's portrait and name), and the first to issue gold coins in India.

3. Inscriptions

Study: Known as epigraphy; the study of old writing used in inscriptions is called palaeography.

Early Scripts: The Harappan script is pictographic and remains undeciphered.

Language: Prakrit was used in the earliest inscriptions; Sanskrit was adopted as an epigraphic medium in the 2nd century AD (e.g., Rudradaman’s Junagadh inscription).

Ashokan Inscriptions: Written mostly in Brahmi script (left to right), as well as Kharosthi (right to left), Greek, and Aramaic scripts.

Notable Examples: Iranian inscriptions (mentioning Hindu/Sindhu), Allahabad Pillar Inscription (associated with Ashoka, Samudragupta, and Jahangir), and various donative records.

4. Literary Evidence

Writing Materials: Written on birch bark (Bhojapatra) and palm leaves (Old Sanskrit).

Vedas (Shruti): Early Vedic texts (Rigveda) comprise prayers; Later Vedic texts comprise rituals, magic, and mythological stories.

Vedangas: Phonetics (Shiksha), ritual (Kalpa), grammar (Vyakarana), etymology (Nirukta), metrics (Chhanda), and astronomy (Jyotisha).

Upanishads: Contain philosophical speculations.

Epics & Puranas: Ramayana, Mahabharata, and the Puranas were largely compiled by 400 AD.

6th Century BC Ritual Texts: Shrautasutras (public sacrifices), Grihyasutras (domestic rituals), and Sulvasutras (measurements for sacrificial altars/early geometry).

Buddhist Texts: Written in Pali—Vinaya Pitaka, Sutta Pitaka, and Abhidhamma Pitaka. Previous birth stories of the Buddha are recorded in the Jatakas.

Jain Texts: Compiled in the 6th century AD (at Vallabhi) in Prakrit.

Secular Literature:

Dharmasutras and Smritis (law books).

Arthashastra of Kautilya (Chandragupta Maurya period).

Ashtadhyayi of Panini (c. 4th/5th century BC) – Sanskrit grammar.

Mahabhashya of Patanjali (c. 150 BC) – commentary on Panini, written during the reign of Pushyamitra Shunga.

Other Classical Works: Plays and works by Bhasa, Shudraka, Kalidasa (Gupta period), and Banabhatta (Harsha's court, 7th century AD) reflect socio-cultural life.

South Indian Texts: Sangam literature (compiled under the patronage of Pandya kings) comprises around 30,000 lines of poetry arranged in eight anthologies (Ettuthokai), including famous collections like Purananuru.

5. Foreign Accounts

Greek & Roman Accounts:

Indica of Megasthenes: Written during Chandragupta Maurya’s reign (321–297 BC); describes Mauryan administration and economic activities.

The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea and Ptolemy’s Geography: Written in Greek; provide valuable data on ancient Indian ports and maritime trade.

Pliny’s Naturalis Historia (Natural History): Written in Latin (1st century AD); laments the drain of Roman gold to India through trade.

Chinese Travellers: Fa-Hien during the reign of Chandragupta II (c. 380–415 AD), Hsuan-Tsang during the reign of Harshavardhana (c. 606–647 AD) – Age of Harsha, and I-Tsing (c. 671–695 AD).

topics.title: The Paleolithic Period
pointers: Earth’s Age: The Earth is over 4,000 million (4 billion) years old.

Quaternary Period (Fourth Stage): Divided into two epochs—the Pleistocene (2,000,000 – 10,000 BC, the Ice Age when early humans appeared) and the Holocene (began ~10,000 years ago with a warmer climate).
Earliest Human Presence in India: Humans appeared in India around 1.4 million years ago, evidenced by early artifacts found at Bori in Maharashtra.
Settlement Pattern: Early humans lived near river valleys and hills where stone was available, avoiding the heavy alluvial plains of the Indus and Ganga due to dense forests and lack of stone.
Palaeolithic Culture (Old Stone Age): Developed during the Pleistocene period (Ice Age) and lasted roughly from 500,000 BC (or 200,000 BC in older texts) to 10,000 BC.
First Palaeolithic Discovery: The first stone tool (a hand-axe) in India was found at Pallavaram (Tamil Nadu) by Robert Bruce Foote in 1863.
Lower Palaeolithic Phase (~500,000 – 50,000 BC): Covered most of the Ice Age; people used hand-axes, cleavers, and choppers.

Lower Palaeolithic Sites: Soan (Sohan) Valley (Punjab, Pakistan), Belan Valley (Mirzapur, UP), Didwana (Rajasthan), Bhimbetka (MP), Narmada Valley (MP/Gujarat), Hunsgi (Karnataka), and Attirampakkam & Pallavaram (Tamil Nadu).

topics.fullNotes:
Transitional Phase: The Mesolithic Age (began around 9000 BC in India, lasting roughly up to 4000 BC) was an intermediate stage between the Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age) and Neolithic (New Stone Age).

Climate Change:

Marked the end of the Ice Age and the beginning of the Holocene epoch, bringing a warmer, drier climate that led to changes in flora and fauna, allowing humans to move into new areas.

Characteristic Tools (Microliths): People used microliths—tiny, sharp stone tools (usually 1 to 5 cm long) like blades, points, lunates, and triangles, often hafted onto wood or bone to make spears and arrows.

Livelihood & Subsistence: Early Mesolithic people survived on hunting, fishing, and food gathering, and later began the domestication of animals (with the dog being the first animal tamed, followed by sheep, goats, and cattle).

Key Geographical Regions: Mesolithic sites are widely distributed across Rajasthan, southern Uttar Pradesh, central and eastern India, and areas south of the Krishna River.

Earliest Evidence of Animal Domestication (~5000 BC): Found at Bagor in Rajasthan (the largest excavated Mesolithic site in India, located on the Kothari River) and Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh.

Other Important Mesolithic Sites:

Langhnaj (Gujarat – famous for human skeletons and burial practices).

Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha, and Damdama (Pratapgarh, Uttar Pradesh – famous for earliest human burials, bone ornaments, and double/triple burials).

Birbhanpur (West Bengal) and Teri sites (Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu – sand dune sites).

Prehistoric Rock Art: Mesolithic people created rock paintings and petroglyphs (rock engravings) depicting hunters, gatherers, geometric symbols, community dancing, and early hints of settled life, notably found at Bhimbetka, Adamgarh, and Pachmarhi (Madhya Pradesh), as well as parts of Jharkhand and Mirzapur (UP).

Bhimbetka Cave Paintings: Feature vivid scenes of archers hunting animals, human figures, and geometric patterns, alongside later paintings showing group dances, horse-riding figures wearing umbrella-like headgear, and musical instruments such as horns, drums, tom-toms, and pipes. (Note: Scenes depicting horse riding and settled agriculture in Bhimbetka belong to the later Chalcolithic/Historic layers painted over earlier Mesolithic art).

topics.fullNotes:
Timeline: In the Indian subcontinent, the Neolithic Age began around 7000 BC in the northwest (Mehrgarh) and around 5000 BC to 1000 BC in other regions, marking the transition from food gathering to food production (agriculture) and settled village life.

Characteristic Tools: People used polished and ground stone tools (especially stone axes/celts), along with microliths and bone tools, allowing them to clear forests and till the soil.

Pottery & Craft: First widespread use of pottery for storing food grains and cooking—initially handmade and later wheel-turned—featuring cord-impressed pottery, black-burnished ware, grey ware, and mat-impressed ware. (Note: Classic Black-and-Red Ware became more prominent in the later Chalcolithic/Megalithic phases, though early forms appeared at sites like Chirand and Piklihal).

Mehrgarh (~7000 BC, Baluchistan, Pakistan): The earliest known Neolithic settlement in the Indian subcontinent (located on the Bolan River); people lived in mud-brick houses and cultivated wheat, barley, and the earliest known cotton in the world.

Kashmiri Neolithic Culture – Burzahom (~2700 BC) & Gufkral (~2000 BC): Located near Srinagar on lakeside/karewa plateaus; characterized by pit dwellings (living in underground pits to survive the cold), an abundance of polished stone and bone tools, coarse grey pottery, and the unique practice of burying domestic dogs with their masters in graves (not caves).

Belan Valley & Gangetic Plains (Uttar Pradesh):

Koldihwa and Mahagara (south of Allahabad/Prayagraj): Provided some of the earliest evidence of rice cultivation (~5000 BC) along with circular huts and cattle pens.

Lahuradewa (Sant Kabir Nagar, UP): Recent excavations show the earliest evidence of rice cultivation in the subcontinent (~8000–7000 BC).

Chirand (Saran district, Bihar): Located at the confluence of the Ganga and Ghaghara rivers; famous for extensive bone and antler tools (second only to Burzahom) and red/black/grey pottery.

South Indian Neolithic Sites (~2000 – 1000 BC): Included Piklihal, Brahmagiri, Maski, Hallur, and Tekkalakota (Karnataka), Utnur and Nagarjunakonda (Andhra Pradesh/Telangana), and Paiyampalli (Tamil Nadu); people were primarily cattle herders (keeping sheep, goats, and cattle) who created distinctive ash mounds (formed by burning seasonal cow-dung camps) and grew ragi (millet) and horse gram.

Eastern & North-Eastern Neolithic Sites: Found in the Garo Hills in Meghalaya and Daojali Hading (Assam), characterized by cord-impressed pottery, double-shouldered stone celts, and early shifting cultivation (jhum) of yams and taro.

topics.fullNotes:
Overview of the Chalcolithic Age: Followed the Neolithic period (roughly 2500 – 700 BC in India) and marked the first use of metal (copper) alongside stone tools; characterized by rural farming communities, widespread Black-and-Red Ware pottery (painted with white linear designs), and worship of the Mother Goddess and bull.

Kayatha Culture (~2450 – 2000 BC, Madhya Pradesh): Located along the Kali Sindh River (a tributary of the Chambal); known as a junior contemporary of the Harappan civilization, featuring sturdy chocolate-slipped pottery and hoards of copper bangles and axes.

Ahar-Banas Culture (~2200 – 1500 BC, Rajasthan): Located in the Banas River valley (Mewar region); key sites include Ahar (ancient name Tambavati or "place having copper," where people practiced copper smelting and lived in stone/mud-brick houses) and Gilund (famous for a large burnt-brick structure). (Note: Ganeshwar in Sikar, Rajasthan is a distinct pre-Harappan/Chalcolithic copper-producing site that supplied copper objects to Harappa).

Malwa Culture (~1700 – 1400 BC, Madhya Pradesh & Maharashtra): Concentrated in the Narmada valley; key sites include Maheshwar, Navdatoli (excavated by H.D. Sankalia; yielded evidence of almost all food grains), Eran, and Nagda; known for the richest Chalcolithic ceramics (buff or cream-slipped pottery painted in black/dark brown).

Savalda Culture (~2000 – 1800 BC, Maharashtra): Concentrated mainly in the Dhule district (Tapi River valley); named after the type-site Savalda and noted for painted pottery featuring weapon motifs and animals.

Jorwe Culture (~1400 – 700 BC, Maharashtra): Covered almost all of modern Maharashtra (except the coastal Konkan strip and parts of Vidarbha); key sites include Prakash (in the Tapi valley), Daimabad (in the Pravara/Godavari valley—the largest Jorwe site, famous for a hoard of heavy bronze sculptures like a chariot, elephant, rhino, and buffalo), and Inamgaon (in the Bhima valley—shows early fortification, irrigation channels, and social stratification).

Prabhas Culture (~1800 – 1400 BC, Gujarat): Located in the coastal Saurashtra region around Prabhas Patan (modern Somnath, the site of the first of the 12 Jyotirlingas); evolved as a Late/Post-Harappan Chalcolithic culture known for distinctive lustrous painted pottery.

Rangpur Culture (~1800 – 1400 BC, Gujarat): Concentrated in the Kathiawar/Saurashtra peninsula (sites like Rangpur and Rojdi); represents a Post-Harappan Chalcolithic phase characterized by Lustrous Red Ware and extensive cultivation of millets (bajra) and rice.

topics.fullNotes:
First Use of Metal: Marked by the use of copper (the first metal used by humans) alongside stone tools, hence called the Copper-Stone (Chalcolithic) Age.

Tools & Weapons: People used small stone tools (microliths) combined with copper tools and weapons such as flat axes, chisels, bangles, and arrowheads.

Pottery: Characterized by Black-and-Red Ware

(wheel-turned and painted with white linear designs); Chalcolithic people were the first to use painted pottery on a wide scale.

Agriculture & Livelihood: Cultivated food grains including wheat, barley, rice, bajra (pearl millet), and pulses (lentil, black gram, green gram); cotton was grown in the black cotton soil of the Deccan, while people in eastern regions (Bihar/Bengal) lived mainly on fish and rice.

Rural Economy: Represented a self-sufficient village-based subsistence economy (the Chalcolithic communities founded the first large villages in India), though they did not practice intensive plough agriculture.

Housing & Settlements: Houses were generally made of mud bricks (burnt bricks were rarely used, except at sites like Gilund) and wattle-and-daub; at Inamgaon (Jorwe culture), large mud houses had five rooms—four rectangular and one circular (likely belonging to a chief).

Settlement Stability & Fortifications: Under the Jorwe culture, settlements became stable and widespread; several settlements like Kayatha, Eran (Madhya Pradesh), and Inamgaon (Maharashtra) were fortified and surrounded by moats.

Religion & Beliefs: People believed in life after death (next birth), venerated terracotta figurines of the Mother Goddess, and worshipped the bull (evidenced by stylized terracotta bull figurines found in Malwa and Rajasthan) as a religious cult.

Burial Practices: Dead bodies were placed in urns and buried under the floor of their houses in a North-to-South position in Maharashtra, whereas in South India they were buried in an East-to-West position; pots and copper objects were deposited in the graves for the dead to use in the next world.

Art, Craft & Metallurgy: Skilled in the art of copper smelting, stone-blade making, bead manufacturing (carnelian, steatite, quartz), and weaving/spinning.

Key Limitations (Exam Focus): Chalcolithic people did not know the art of writing, did not live in cities (unlike the Bronze Age Harappans), and suffered from a high rate of infant mortality (evidenced by a large number of child burials in western Maharashtra).

topics.fullNotes:
Discovery & Nomenclature: Sir John Marshall first coined the term "Indus Valley Civilization"; Daya Ram Sahni excavated Harappa in 1921, and R.D. Banerji excavated Mohenjo-daro in 1922.

Mesopotamian Name & Status: Mesopotamian texts referred to the Indus region as Meluhha; it was a vast Bronze Age civilization and marked the first urbanization in the Indian subcontinent.

Three Chronological Phases:

Early / Pre-Harappan Phase (~3300 – 2600 BC): Formative rural phase (e.g., Kot Diji, Amri, Kalibangan-I).

Mature Harappan Phase (~2600 – 1900 BC): Peak urban phase with large cities, standardized bricks, and long-distance trade.

Late Harappan Phase (~1900 – 1300 BC): Decline of urban centers and return to rural settlements (e.g., Rangpur, Rojdi, Cemetery H).

Geographical Extent: Stretched from Manda (Jammu, North) to Daimabad (Maharashtra, South), and from Alamgirpur (Uttar Pradesh, East) to Sutkagendor (Baluchistan, West).

Harappan Town Planning:

Citadel / Acropolis and Lower Town: Cities were divided into a raised western Citadel (for public buildings and elites) and a larger eastern Lower Town (for common citizens), except Chanhudaro (no citadel) and Dholavira (3 parts).

Grid System & Houses: Streets were laid out in a grid pattern intersecting at right angles; houses were built of standardized burnt bricks (ratio 4:2:1), with doors and windows opening onto side lanes rather than main streets for privacy.

Monumental Structures: Famous for Granaries (Mohenjo-daro and Harappa), the Great Bath (Mohenjo-daro, used for ritual bathing), fire altars at Kalibangan (Rajasthan), and large stone-built water tanks/reservoirs at Dholavira (Gujarat).

Drainage System: Featured an advanced, covered underground drainage system made of burnt bricks with inspection manholes at regular intervals.

Agriculture & Subsistence Base:

Ecological Diversity: Thrived across alluvial plains, plateaus, and sea coasts, supported by a diverse subsistence base combining farming, animal husbandry, hunting, and riverine/marine food resources.

Crop Diversification: Practiced both Rabi (winter) and Kharif (summer) cropping, cultivating wheat, barley, peas, chickpeas, sesame, and mustard; rice cultivation is evidenced at Rangpur and Lothal (Gujarat).

Cotton: Harappans were the earliest to produce cotton, which the Greeks later called Sindon (derived from Sindh).

Ploughing & Irrigation: Evidence of a ploughed field comes from Kalibangan, while terracotta models of the plough were found at Banawali (Haryana) and Bahawalpur (Cholistan, Pakistan); traces of irrigation canals were discovered at Shortughai (Afghanistan).

Domestication of Animals & Marine Resources:

Domesticated Animals: Reared cattle (for milk and meat), buffalo, sheep, goat, pig, camel, elephant, dog, cat, and ass.

Wild Animals & Exceptions (Exam Focus): The Indian one-horned rhinoceros was well known (evidenced by skeletal remains at Amri and depictions on seals, including the Pashupati seal), horse remains are rare and disputed (found at Surkotada in Gujarat), and the lion was not known to the Harappans.

Marine Resources: Coastal sites in Gujarat exploited marine catfish, molluscs, and dried fish (which was also traded inland to sites like Harappa).

topics.title: Harappan Economy, Trade, Art & Craft
pointers: Pottery & Painting: Harappans used well-fired, wheel-turned Red-and-Black Ware (red slip with black painted geometric, floral, and animal motifs) alongside plain, perforated, and polychrome pottery.

Metals & Metallurgy: Known as a Bronze Age civilization; artisans were skilled in bronze ware (made by mixing copper with tin using the lost-wax / cire perdue technique) and worked with gold, silver, copper, bronze, and lead, though iron was completely unknown.

Bead Industry & Jewellery: Chanhudaro and Lothal were major centers of an elaborate bead-making and shell industry; ornaments and jewellery (necklaces, fillets, armlets, rings) were worn by both men and women and crafted from gold, silver, copper, bronze, faience, shell, ivory...
Textiles & Cotton: Spinning and weaving were widespread (evidenced by spindle whorls); Harappans were the earliest to produce cotton, which the Greeks later called Sindon (after Sindh).

Weights & Measures: Used standardized cubical weights made of chert (following a binary system in lower denominations—1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64—and decimal system in higher multiples of 16); linear measurement scales of shell, ivory, and bronze were found at Lothal, Mohenj...

Transport (Carts & Boats): Inland transport relied on bullock carts with solid wheels (evidenced by terracotta toy carts and bronze models from Harappa and Chanhudaro), while riverine and sea trade used flat-bottomed boats (depicted on seals and terracotta amulets).
Nature of Trade & Absence of Coins: Conducted brisk internal and foreign trade; metallic coins were not used

Mesopotamian Trade & Sargon of Akkad: Trade with Mesopotamia (Sumer) is confirmed by the inscriptions of King Sargon of Akkad (~2350 BC), which mention ships arriving from Meluhha (the Indus region), and by Harappan seals discovered at Mesopotamian cities like Ur, Kish, and Susa.
topics.fullNotes:
Pottery & Painting: Harappans used well-fired, wheel-turned Red-and-Black Ware (red slip with black painted geometric, floral, and animal motifs) alongside plain, perforated, and polychrome pottery.

Metals & Metallurgy: Known as a Bronze Age civilization; artisans were skilled in bronze ware (made by mixing copper with tin using the lost-wax / cire perdue technique) and worked with gold, silver, copper, bronze, and lead, though iron was completely unknown.

Bead Industry & Jewellery: Chanhudaro and Lothal were major centers of an elaborate bead-making and shell industry; ornaments and jewellery (necklaces, fillets, armlets, rings) were worn by both men and women and crafted from gold, silver, copper, bronze, faience, shell, ivory, and semi-precious stones like carnelian (especially etched carnelian beads).

Textiles & Cotton: Spinning and weaving were widespread (evidenced by spindle whorls); Harappans were the earliest to produce cotton, which the Greeks later called Sindon (after Sindh).

Weights & Measures: Used standardized cubical weights made of chert (following a binary system in lower denominations—1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64—and decimal system in higher multiples of 16); linear measurement scales of shell, ivory, and bronze were found at Lothal, Mohenjo-daro, and Harappa.

Transport (Carts & Boats): Inland transport relied on bullock carts with solid wheels (evidenced by terracotta toy carts and bronze models from Harappa and Chanhudaro), while riverine and sea trade used flat-bottomed boats (depicted on seals and terracotta amulets).

Nature of Trade & Absence of Coins: Conducted brisk internal and foreign trade; metallic coins were not used

—all exchanges operated strictly through the barter system.

Mesopotamian Trade & Sargon of Akkad: Trade with Mesopotamia (Sumer) is confirmed by the inscriptions of King Sargon of Akkad (~2350 BC), which mention ships arriving from Meluhha (the Indus region), and by Harappan seals discovered at Mesopotamian cities like Ur, Kish, and Susa.

Seaports & Coastal Outlets: Maritime trade operated through key coastal outlets and seaports including Lothal (featured the world’s earliest artificial tidal dockyard), Sutkagendor, Sotkakoh (Makran coast), Balakot, Rangpur, and Allahdino.

Major Imports (Raw Materials & Sources): Gold (Kolar Gold Fields/Karnataka, Afghanistan, and Persia), Silver (Afghanistan and Persia/Iran), Copper (Khetri mines in Rajasthan and Oman/Arabia), Tin (Afghanistan and Central Asia), Lapis Lazuli (Badakhshan, Afghanistan), Sapphire & Turquoise (Afghanistan/Persia), Steatite (Persia/Iran and Rajasthan), Jade (Central Asia/Pamir region), and Amethyst (Maharashtra/Deccan).

Major Exports: Cotton goods, agricultural products (wheat, barley, oilseeds), terracotta figurines, pottery, ivory work, shell objects, and carnelian beads.

Harappan Seals: Over 2,000 steatite seals (mostly square, some cylindrical/button-shaped) have been found, engraved with pictographic script and animals like the unicorn, humped bull, elephant, tiger, and Indian one-horned rhinoceros (used for stamping trade goods and identity).

Bronze Dancing Girl (Mohenjo-daro): A 10.8 cm figure cast via the lost-wax technique, depicting a naked girl wearing bangles and a necklace in the rhythmic tribhanga dancing posture (three-bend stance at the neck, waist, and knee, with her right hand on her hip and left hand resting on her thigh).

Steatite Bearded Man / Priest-King (Mohenjo-daro): Draped in a trefoil-patterned shawl with half-closed meditative eyes.

Red Sandstone Male Torso (Harappa): Known for its realistic anatomical modeling and socket holes for attaching the head and arms.

Terracotta Art & Toys: Made abundant terracotta figurines of the Mother Goddess, animals, whistles, rattles, carts with movable heads, and terracotta toys for children.

Favourite Pastimes (Dice & Gambling): Gambling and dice games were a favourite pastime among Harappans (evidenced by cubical terracotta and ivory dice found at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa), alongside hunting, fishing, bull-fighting, and music/dance.

topics.fullNotes:
Cosmopolitan Society: Harappan cities had a cosmopolitan, multi-ethnic population (comprising Proto-Australoid, Mediterranean, Alpine, and Mongoloid racial elements) living peacefully together; this cultural diversity is reflected in their varied religious beliefs, regional cult practices (such as Mother Goddess worship in the Indus valley versus fire altars in Rajasthan/Gujarat), and multiple burial methods.

Absence of Temples & Idolatry: Unlike contemporary Mesopotamian and Egyptian civilizations, no temples or monumental religious structures have been discovered at any Harappan site (except for the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro, which was likely used for ritual purification bathing, and fire altars at Kalibangan and Lothal).

Secular Polity: Due to the absence of temples, historians believe Harappan society was primarily ruled by a class of merchants rather than priests, though a priestly class likely performed rituals.

Worship of the Mother Goddess (Fertility Cult): Excavations have yielded numerous terracotta figurines of women; one famous seal from Harappa shows a plant growing out of the embryo/womb of a woman, representing the Earth Goddess (Goddess of Fertility) connected with the origin and growth of plants.

Pashupati Mahadeva (Proto-Shiva): A famous steatite seal from Mohenjo-daro depicts a male deity with three horned heads sitting in a yogic posture (padmasana) on a low throne, surrounded by four wild animals—an elephant and a tiger on his right, and a rhinoceros and a buffalo on his left, with two deer (antelopes) beneath his throne; Sir John Marshall identified him as Proto-Shiva (Pashupati, Lord of Animals).

Phallus (Linga) & Yoni Worship: Numerous polished stone symbols resembling the phallus (linga) and female sex organs (yoni) have been found at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, indicating the early prevalence of fertility and Shiva-Shakti worship (later mentioned in the Rig Veda as Shishnadevas or worshippers of the phallus).

Tree & Nature Worship: Harappans worshipped nature and trees, most notably the Peepal tree (Ficus religiosa), which is depicted on a famous seal with a deity standing between its branches and seven worshippers standing below.

Animal Worship: Animals were revered either as deities or as vehicles (vahanas) of gods—the most sacred were the one-horned animal (unicorn) and the humped bull (zebu), followed by the elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, and snake.

Fire Altars & Ritual Sacrifices: Rows of fire altars (havan kundas) containing ash, charcoal, and animal bones have been excavated at Kalibangan (Rajasthan), Lothal (Gujarat), and Banawali (Haryana), proving the practice of fire worship and animal sacrifice.

Amulets, Charms & Shamanism: Large numbers of amulets and talismans made of terracotta, faience, and copper have been found, suggesting that Harappans believed in ghosts, evil spirits, and magical charms to ward off harm.

Swastika & Sacred Symbols: The Swastika and wheel motifs appear frequently on Harappan seals and pottery, symbolizing the Sun and good fortune.

Burial Practices & Belief in Afterlife: Harappans buried their dead (generally in a North-South orientation with the head toward the north) along with grave goods like pottery, ornaments, copper mirrors, and beads—indicating a strong belief in life after death.

Complete / Extended Burial: Whole body laid flat in a rectangular pit (most common, e.g., Cemetery R-37 at Harappa).

Fractional Burial: Collection of bones buried in an urn after the body was exposed to wild animals and birds.

Post-Cremation Burial: Ashes and charred bones collected in urns after cremation and buried.

Special Burial Sites: Double/pair burials (male and female together) at Lothal; coffin burial at Harappa; dog buried with human at Ropar (Punjab); and pot/urn burials at Kalibangan and Surkotada.

topics.fullNotes:
Nature of Political Organization: While the exact political structure remains uncertain due to the undeciphered script, the remarkable uniformity in town planning, brick ratios (4:2:1), weights, measures, and pottery across a vast region proves the existence of a strong, centralized authority.

Rule by Merchant Class (R.S. Sharma’s View): Because no temples, royal palaces, or grand tombs have been found (unlike Egypt and Mesopotamia), historians like R.S. Sharma suggest that the Harappan state was likely ruled by a class of wealthy merchants and traders rather than priests or warrior kings.

Priest-King & Twin Capitals View (Piggott & Wheeler): Stuart Piggott and Mortimer Wheeler proposed that the civilization was ruled by a priest-king or centralized autocratic bureaucracy operating from twin capitals (Harappa and Mohenjo-daro).

Republican / Oligarchic View (Hunter & Kosambi): Hunter and D.D. Kosambi suggested a republican or oligarchic system governed by committees of urban elites or civic councils.

Absence of Standing Army & Weapons: Very few offensive weapons (like swords, shields, or helmets) have been excavated—only basic copper/bronze daggers, spears, and arrowheads—indicating that Harappan society was largely peaceful, commercial, and focused on trade rather than military conquest.

Civic Administration: Municipal authorities efficiently managed urban infrastructure, including street grid layouts, covered drainage systems, public granaries, standardized weights, and defensive citadel walls.

Origin & Invention of Script: The Harappans invented the art of writing independently in the Indian subcontinent (earliest specimens discovered in 1853 by Alexander Cunningham, and the complete script came to light by 1923).

Pictographic & Logo-Syllabic Nature: The script is pictographic (consisting of pictures of birds, fish, humans, and geometric signs) and logo-syllabic (each symbol stands for a word or syllable rather than an alphabet).

Number of Signs: There are roughly 400 to 450 basic signs (with around 250–375 core characters); the fish symbol is the most frequently occurring sign.

Writing Direction (Boustrophedon Style): The script was generally written from right to left in the first line, and left to right in the second line—a style known as Boustrophedon (evidenced by crowding of signs on the left side of seals).

Mediums & Inscriptions: Unlike Mesopotamians (who wrote long records on clay tablets), Harappans wrote short inscriptions (average length of 5 signs, longest single inscription has 26 signs) on steatite seals, copper tablets, pottery, ivory rods, and terracotta.

Dholavira Signboard: A unique, large 10-sign inscription made of white gypsum paste inlaid on a wooden board was discovered near the north gate of the citadel at Dholavira (Gujarat), likely serving as a public signboard.

Undeciphered Status: The Harappan script remains undeciphered to this day due to the brevity of inscriptions and the lack of a bilingual text (like Egypt’s Rosetta Stone), though computer-aided studies (such as by Iravatham Mahadevan and Asko Parpola) suggest a link to a Proto-Dravidian language family.

Bisht (1990); UNESCO World Heritage Site; unique for being divided into three parts (Citadel, Middle Town, and Lower Town) instead of two; renowned for sophisticated stone-built water harvesting reservoirs, a stadium, and a 10-sign signboard inscription.

Banawali (Rangoi / dried Saraswati River, Hissar, Haryana): Excavated by R.S. Bisht (1974); displays all three phases (Pre-Harappan, Mature, and Late Harappan); yielded a terracotta model of a plough, high-quality barley, radial streets, and lacked a grid pattern and systematic drainage.

Rakhigarhi (Ghaggar-Hakra plain, Hissar, Haryana): Excavated by Amarendra Nath and Vasant Shinde; recognized as the largest Harappan site in the entire Indian subcontinent (larger than Mohenjo-daro), yielding pre-Harappan and mature Harappan settlements and DNA evidence.

Surkotada (Kutch, Gujarat): Excavated by J.P. Joshi (1964); the only Harappan site where actual skeletal remains of a horse have been found, along with pot burials and a stone-fortified citadel.

Sutkagendor (Dasht River, Baluchistan, Pakistan): Excavated by Aurel Stein (1929); the westernmost Harappan site, originally a coastal port city that traded with Babylon/Mesopotamia before silting up.

Alamgirpur (Hindon River, Meerut, Uttar Pradesh): Excavated by Y.D. Sharma (1958); marks the easternmost boundary of the Harappan Civilization and belongs mainly to the Late Harappan phase.

Manda (Chenab River, Jammu): Excavated by J.P. Joshi (1982); marks the northernmost boundary of the Harappan Civilization.

Daimabad (Pravara River, Maharashtra): Excavated by B.P. Bopardikar; marks the southernmost boundary of the Harappan Civilization and yielded a famous hoard of four heavy bronze sculptures (chariot, elephant, rhinoceros, and buffalo).

Ropar / Rupnagar (Sutlej River, Punjab, India): Excavated by Y.D. Sharma (1953); the first Harappan site excavated in independent India, famous for the unique burial of a dog buried beneath a human grave.

Rangpur (Madar River, Gujarat): Excavated by M.S. Vats and S.R. Rao; an important Late Harappan port and agricultural site where rice husks were discovered alongside Lothal.

Amri (Indus River, Sindh, Pakistan): Excavated by N.G. Majumdar (1929); a major Pre-Harappan and Mature Harappan site that yielded actual skeletal remains of the Indian one-horned rhinoceros.

topics.fullNotes:
Timeline of Decline: The Mature Harappan phase began to decline around 1900 BC and largely disappeared as an urban civilization by 1750 BC, transitioning into localized rural Late Harappan cultures (such as Cemetery H, Jhukar, and Rangpur phases).

Gradual Transformation vs. Sudden Collapse: Modern archaeologists agree that the civilization did not end overnight in a single catastrophe, but experienced a gradual de-urbanization—marked by the breakdown of long-distance trade, abandonment of standardized weights/script, decline in civic upkeep, and eastward/southward migration of populations.

Climate Change & Aridification (Gurdip Singh & Modern Paleoclimatology): Weakening of the Indian summer monsoon around 2000–1900 BC caused prolonged droughts and increased aridity, severely reducing agricultural yields that sustained large urban populations.

Drying Up of the Ghaggar-Hakra / Saraswati River (D.P. Agrawal & Sood): Tectonic shifts captured the Sutlej (diverting it into the Indus) and the Yamuna (diverting it into the Ganga), causing the mighty Ghaggar-Hakra river system—along which the highest density of Harappan sites stood—to dry up.

Recurrent Floods & Tectonic Uplift (M.R. Sahni, Robert Raikes & George Dales): Tectonic movements near the Indus delta created natural dams that caused the Indus River to flood Mohenjo-daro repeatedly (evidenced by thick layers of silt) and shifted river courses away from major cities.

Ecological Degradation & Deforestation (Walter Fairservis): Overgrazing by cattle, excessive deforestation for baking millions of burnt bricks and smelting copper, and soil salinization from over-irrigation exhausted the fragile ecosystem.

Decline of Mesopotamian Trade (Shereen Ratnagar): Around 1900 BC, the collapse of the Ur III dynasty in Mesopotamia disrupted the lucrative overseas trade with Meluhha, crippling the merchant-driven urban economy of Harappan cities.

Epidemic / Malaria Outbreak (K.A.R. Kennedy): Skeletal studies from Mohenjo-daro show signs of chronic anemia and infectious diseases (like malaria caused by stagnant floodwaters), weakening the urban population.

Aryan Invasion Theory — Now Rejected (Mortimer Wheeler & Stuart Piggott): Wheeler originally argued that Indo-Aryan invaders destroyed Harappan cities (citing Rig Vedic references to Indra as Purandara, "destroyer of forts," and unburied skeletons at Mohenjo-daro); however, modern archaeology rejects this theory because the skeletons date to different periods with no signs of warfare, and cities had already been abandoned centuries before the Aryans arrived.

topics.fullNotes:
1. Shruti vs. Smriti & The Four-Fold Vedic Architecture

Vedic literature is primarily classified as Shruti ("that which is heard"), believed to be eternal truths revealed to ancient sages (Rishis) during deep meditation, rather than human compositions (Apaurusheya). It is distinct from Smriti ("that which is remembered"), which includes later human-authored texts like the Epics (Ramayana, Mahabharata), Puranas, and Dharmashastras.

Each of the four Vedas is built in four chronological and thematic layers:

Samhita (The Core Mantras): Collections of metric hymns, prayers, and benedictions. They represent the earliest, devotional phase of Vedic religion.

Brahmana (Ritual Manuals): Written in prose, these act as "how-to" guides for priests. They explain the exact procedures, symbolic meanings, and theology behind complex sacrifices (Yajnas). (e.g., Shatapatha Brahmana, Aitareya Brahmana).

Aranyaka (Forest Treatises): Serving as a bridge between ritualism and philosophy, these texts were taught in the solitude of forests (Aranya) to hermits and ascetics (Vanaprasthas). They replace physical animal sacrifices with symbolic meditation and inner rituals.

Upanishad (Philosophical Conclusions): Literally meaning "sitting near" (a teacher), these 108+ texts form Vedanta ("the end of the Vedas"). They shift the focus entirely from external rituals to internal realization—exploring Brahman (the Ultimate Reality), Atman (the individual soul), Karma, and Moksha (liberation).

2. Early Vedic Age (1500 BC – 1000 BC): The Rig Vedic World

Geography & Society: Centered around the Sapta Sindhu (land of seven rivers—Indus and its tributaries). Society was semi-nomadic, pastoral, and tribal (Jana).

The Rig Veda Samhita:

Contains 1,028 hymns (Suktas) divided into 10 books (Mandalas).

Mandalas 2 to 7 are the oldest ("Family Books"), while Mandalas 1 and 10 were added later (Mandala 10 contains the famous Purusha Sukta, which first mentions the four-fold Varna system).

Chief Deities: Indra (war/rain), Agni (fire, the mediator between humans and gods), and Varuna (cosmic order).

Evolution of the 16 Priestly Classes:

Originally, complex Soma rituals required 16 specialized priests divided into four groups: Hotri (reciter of Rig Veda), Udgatri (chanter of Sama Veda), Adhvaryu (performer of Yajur Veda rituals), and Brahmana (the chief supervisor who knew all Vedas).

Over time, the supervisory Brahmana class absorbed the supreme ritual authority and consolidated into a distinct hereditary Varna.

3. Later Vedic Age (1000 BC – 600 BC): Expansion & Complexity

As Aryans moved eastward into the fertile Indo-Gangetic plain (Kuru-Panchala region), society shifted from pastoralism to settled agriculture. Kingdoms (Janapadas) replaced tribes.

Detailed Breakdown of the Three Later Vedas

Socio-Political Shifts

The Brahmana–Kshatriya Alliance: To legitimize their new territorial power over commoners (Vaishyas) and laborers (Shudras), Kshatriya kings relied on Brahmanas to perform grand, multi-day state sacrifices:

Rajasuya: Royal consecration ceremony conferring supreme power.

Ashvamedha: Horse sacrifice symbolizing unquestioned territorial sovereignty.

Vajapeya: Chariot race ritual to rejuvenate the king's strength.

Rise of Upanishadic Thought & Heterodox Sects (6th Century BC):

Royal courts—especially in the Panchala and Videha kingdoms (under philosopher-kings like Pravahana Jaivali and Janaka)—became centers of philosophical debate.

The Mundaka Upanishad explicitly criticized sacrifices as "unsafe boats" that cannot carry one across the ocean of rebirth.

This anti-ritual, anti-caste ferment paved the way for Shramana (heterodox) movements like Buddhism (Gautama Buddha) and Jainism (Mahavira), which rejected the infallibility of the Vedas altogether.

4. Oral Preservation, Writing & Historical Timeline

Why No Early Manuscripts Exist: The Vedas were preserved through strict oral memorization techniques (Pathas—like Jata-patha and Ghana-patha) that ensured zero syllable errors over millennia. Writing was initially viewed as impure for sacred Shruti texts.

Arrival of Writing (6th – 2nd Century BC): While the Indus Valley script (2600–1900 BC) remained undeciphered and fell out of use, alphabetic/abugida writing re-emerged around the 6th century BC (referenced by grammarian Panini) and reached pan-Indian standardization under the Mauryan Empire (3rd–2nd century BC) via Ashoka’s Brahmi and Kharosthi edicts.

Oldest Surviving Manuscripts (11th Century AD): Due to India's tropical climate degrading palm-leaf and birch-bark manuscripts, the oldest surviving physical manuscript of the Rig Veda dates to around 1040 AD (preserved in Nepal).

Adi Shankaracharya (c. 788 – 820 AD): Born in Kalady (Kerala), he synthesized the Upanishads, Brahma Sutras, and Bhagavad Gita (the Prasthanatrayi) into Advaita Vedanta (non-dualism). By establishing four Mathas (monastic centers) in the four corners of India (Sringeri, Puri, Dwarka, Joshimath), he countered the decline of Vedic traditions and unified diverse sects under a cohesive philosophical framework.

rows: Contains 1,875 verses (mostly borrowed from the Rig Veda) set to musical melodies ( Samans ). Considered the origin of Indian classical music .
Shukla (White): Clear separation of mantras and prose. Krishna (Black): Mixed mantras and commentary.
A manual for the Adhvaryu priest. Details exact measurements for fire altars (leading to early Indian geometry via the Sulvasutras ) and royal sacrifices.
Reflects the beliefs of the common people rather than just priests. Contains charms against diseases/demons, herbal medicine ( origin of Ayurveda ), and marriage/burial hymns.

1. Core Classification: Shruti vs. Smriti

Shruti ("That which is heard"):

Considered eternal, divine revelations heard by ancient sages (Rishis) during meditation. It comprises the four Vedas and their sub-layers.

Smriti ("That which is remembered"): Supplementary texts composed by human authors based on Vedic teachings. This includes the Vedangas (limbs of the Veda), Upavedas, Puranas, Dharmashastras, and the Itihasas (Ramayana and Mahabharata).

2. The Four Vedas (Samhitas)

Each Veda serves a distinct liturgical and cultural function in ancient Indian society:

3. The Four Structural Layers of Every Veda

Each of the four Vedas is systematically divided into four progressive sections:

Samhita: The foundational collection of mantras, hymns, and benedictions.

Brahmana: Prose commentaries explaining the rules, symbolism, and theology of Vedic rituals.

Aranyaka: "Forest treatises" meant for hermits and ascetics, shifting focus from physical sacrifices to symbolic meditation.

Upanishad: The philosophical conclusion (Vedanta), exploring the nature of the soul (Atman), Ultimate Reality (Brahman), Karma, and liberation (Moksha).

4. Auxiliary Literature (Vedangas & Upavedas)

To preserve, pronounce, and apply the Vedas accurately, six auxiliary disciplines (Vedangas) and four applied sciences (Upavedas) were developed:

Six Vedangas: Shiksha (Phonetics), Chhanda (Metrics), Vyakarana (Grammar), Nirukta (Etymology), Jyotisha (Astronomy/Calendar), and Kalpa (Ritual procedures).

Four Upavedas: Ayurveda (Medicine), Dhanurveda (Archery/Warfare), Gandharvaveda (Music/Dance), and Shilpaveda (Architecture/Crafts).

topics.fullNotes:
1. Grand Public & Royal Sacrifices (Shrauta Yajnas)

Performed by kings, nobles, and wealthy householders with the help of multiple specialized priests using three sacred fires.

A. Major Royal / Political Sacrifices

Rajasuya: The Royal Consecration sacrifice performed when a king ascended the throne, believed to imbue the ruler with divine power and legitimacy.

Ashvamedha: The Horse Sacrifice performed by an ambitious king to assert supreme territorial sovereignty. A royal horse was let loose to wander freely for a year; any rival king who stopped it had to fight, while those who let it pass acknowledged the king's overlordship.

Vajapeya: The "Drink of Strength" sacrifice featuring a symbolic chariot race in which the royal chariot was made to win against kinsmen, rejuvenating the king's authority and vitality.

B. Soma Sacrifices (Soma Yajnas)

Rituals centered around extracting, offering, and drinking the sacred Soma juice:

Agnishtoma: The foundational one-day Soma sacrifice offered to Agni (the fire god), forming the model for all other Soma rituals.

Atiratra & Aptoryama: Extended, complex variations of the Soma sacrifice lasting multiple days and nights.

C. Fire & Oblation Sacrifices (Havir Yajnas)

Simple offerings of milk, ghee, grains, and cakes into the sacred fire without Soma:

Agnihotra: A simple, daily morning and evening milk/ghee offering made to Agni and Surya.

Darshapurnamasa: Rituals performed every New Moon (Darsha) and Full Moon (Purnamasa).

Chaturmasya: Seasonal sacrifices performed every four months to mark the changing seasons and ensure agricultural prosperity.

2. Domestic Sacrifices (Grihya Yajnas & Panchamahayajnas)

Performed by an individual householder (Grihastha) using a single domestic fire (Grihyagni) for family welfare and daily spiritual duty.

The Five Daily Great Sacrifices (Panchamahayajnas)

Every householder was expected to perform five simple daily offerings to repay cosmic debts:

Brahma Yajna: Studying and teaching the Vedas (offering to the sages).

Deva Yajna: Pouring ghee into the household fire (offering to the gods).

Pitri Yajna: Offering water and food (Tarpana/Shraddha) to ancestors.

Bhuta Yajna: Setting aside food for animals, birds, and insects.

Manushya (Nri) Yajna: Feeding guests, travelers, and the needy (Atithi Seva).

3. Symbolic & Philosophical Sacrifices (Upanishadic Shift)

By the Later Vedic and Upanishadic periods, complex animal and material sacrifices (Pashubandha, Purushamedha—which became purely symbolic) were reinterpreted inward as Jnana Yajna (sacrifice of ignorance through knowledge) and Prana Agnihotra (offering breath and sensory control as inner oblations).

topics.fullNotes:
The arrival and settlement of Indo-Aryan speaking people in northwestern India. Reconstructed primarily from the Rig Veda (Mandalas 2 to 7), this era was characterized by a semi-nomadic, pastoral lifestyle, kinship-based tribal governance, and naturalistic religion.

1. Origins, Linguistic Group & Archaeological Evidence

Linguistic Identity: "Arya" is a linguistic group (Indo-European / Indo-Iranian language family), not a biological race. The term Arya appears 36 times in the Rig Veda, signifying cultural/linguistic affinity rather than ethnicity.

The "Aryan Invasion" vs. Migration Debate:

Early colonial historians (like Mortimer Wheeler) proposed a violent Aryan Invasion that destroyed the Indus Valley Civilization (citing the battle-god Indra as Purandara, destroyer of forts).

Modern historians and archaeological evidence reject a sudden mass invasion in favor of gradual waves of migration from the Eurasian steppes (Andronovo culture) via Bactria–Margiana (BMAC) into northwestern India around 1500 BC.

West Asian Inscriptional Evidence (Tracing the Migration Route):

Hittite Inscription (Anatolia/Turkey, c. 19th–17th century BC): Earliest traces of Indo-European speakers in West Asia.

Kassite Inscription (Iraq/Mesopotamia, c. 1600 BC): Mentions Indo-Aryan names and horse-related terms.

Boghazkoi Inscription (Turkey, c. 1400 BC): A peace treaty between the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I and the Mitanni king Shattiwaza that invokes four classic Rig Vedic deities as witnesses: Indra, Varuna, Mitra, and Nasatya (Ashvins). This proves Indo-Aryans passed through West Asia before entering India.

2. Geography & Rivers

Early Vedic Aryans settled in the Sapta Sindhu ("Land of Seven Rivers"), covering eastern Afghanistan, Punjab, and parts of western Uttar Pradesh.

(Note: The Ganga is mentioned only once in the 10th Mandala, and the Yamuna three times, showing they had not yet expanded deep into the Gangetic plains.)

3. Political Structure & Administration

Political Organization (Hierarchy from Base to Top)

Kula (Family) → headed by Kulapa

Grama (Village/Clan) → headed by Gramani

Vis (Clan/Canton) → headed by Vishpati

Jana (Tribe) → headed by Rajan (Chieftain/Gopati)

Rashtra (Territory—emerging concept, not yet fully territorial)

Key Political Positions & Officers

Rajan: Tribal chief who protected cattle and led wars; power was limited by tribal assemblies.

Purohita: Chief royal priest, advisor, and spiritual guide (e.g., Vasishtha and Vishvamitra).

Senani: Commander of the tribal militia (there was no regular standing army).

Vrajapati: Officer in charge of pasture lands; led Gramanis into battle.

Spasa: Spies who kept watch over public conduct and rival tribes.

Jivagribha & Ugra: Police-like officials responsible for catching criminals.

Madhyamasi: Mediator in local disputes.

Tribal Assemblies

Sabha: Exclusive council of elders and elites; performed judicial functions.

Samiti: General assembly of the entire tribe; elected or approved the Rajan.

Vidatha: Oldest assembly for religious, military, and booty-distribution decisions; women participated actively in both Sabha and Vidatha.

Gana: Assembly of troops/republican clan elders.

4. The Battle of Ten Kings (Dasharajna War)

Location: Banks of the river Parushni (Ravi).

Cause: King Sudas of the Bharata tribe replaced his chief priest Vishvamitra with sage Vasishtha.

Combatants: Angered by his dismissal, Vishvamitra organized a confederacy of 10 tribes—5 Aryan tribes (Puru, Yadu, Turvasha, Anu, Druhyu—known as the Panchajana) and 5 non-Aryan tribes (Alina, Paktha, Bhalanas, Shiva, Vishanin)—against Sudas.

Outcome: King Sudas decisively defeated the confederacy, establishing the supremacy of the Bharata tribe (from which India takes the name Bharatavarsha). Later, the Bharatas merged with the defeated Purus to form the powerful Kuru dynasty.

5. Economy

Mainly Pastoral: Cattle rearing was the primary occupation. Cows were the standard unit of exchange and wealth (Gomat = wealthy man; Gavishti = war/search for cows; Duhitri = daughter/one who milks; Goghna = guest for whom cattle are killed/served).

Secondary Agriculture: Practiced mainly for subsistence using wooden ploughshares (Langala). Only one grain, Yava (barley), is prominently mentioned.

Crafts & Trade: Carpenters (Takshan), chariot-makers (Rathakara), weavers, potters, and metalworkers (Karmara working with Ayas—copper/bronze; iron was unknown). Trade was conducted via barter using cows and gold ornaments (Nishka).

Taxation: No formal tax system existed; people gave voluntary offerings called Bali.

6. Society, Purusha Sukta & Position of Women

Kinship & Egalitarianism: Society was patriarchal (Pitrikula) yet relatively egalitarian. Early divisions were occupational rather than birth-based.

Purusha Sukta (10th Mandala, Rig Veda): Added toward the very end of the Early Vedic period, this hymn symbolically describes the origin of the four Varnas from the cosmic being (Purusha): Brahmanas (mouth), Kshatriyas/Rajanyas (arms), Vaishyas (thighs), and Shudras (feet). However, untouchability and rigid caste endogamy did not exist yet.

Position of Women:

Respected status; girls received education and underwent the sacred thread ceremony (Upanayana).

No child marriage or Sati (only a symbolic ritual of lying beside the deceased husband existed).

Niyoga: Widow remarriage was permitted, specifically levirate marriage (Niyoga), where a childless widow could marry her deceased husband’s younger brother to bear a child.

Brahmavadinis: Learned women who remained lifelong scholars and composed Rig Vedic hymns—notably Lopamudra, Ghosha, Apala, Vishvavara, and Sikata.

Food & Amusement:

Food: Milk, ghee, curd, barley cakes (Apupa), vegetables, fruits, and occasional meat (a cow was considered Aghnya—not to be killed—except for honored guests). Drinks included Soma (sacred ritual drink) and Sura (fermented secular liquor).

Amusement: Chariot racing, horse racing, dicing/gambling, music (flute, lute, drums), and communal dancing.

7. Religion

Naturalistic Polytheism & Henotheism: Early Vedic people personified forces of nature (rain, fire, wind, dawn) as gods. Max Müller termed their worship Henotheism (Kathenotheism)—treating whichever deity was being prayed to at that moment as the supreme god.

Mode of Worship: Prayers (Stuti) and simple fire sacrifices (Yajnas) offering milk, ghee, and grains to gain material rewards (Praja = children, Pashu = cattle, Vira = brave sons, and health)—not spiritual Moksha. Temples and idol worship were completely absent.

Key Deities:

Indra (Purandara): Most important god (250 hymns); god of storm, rain, and war.

Agni: Fire god (200 hymns); mediator between humans and gods.

Varuna: Guardian of Rita (cosmic and moral order); punisher of sin.

Soma: Lord of plants and sacred sacrificial drink (9th Mandala).

Other Deities: Surya, Savitr (solar deity of the Gayatri Mantra), Pushan (protector of cattle and roads), Rudra (storm/healing deity), and goddesses Ushas (dawn), Aditi, and Saraswati.

8. Key Historical & Literary Personalities Summary

Kings: Sudas (victor of Dasharajna), Divodasa (Bharata ancestor), Trasadasyu (Puru ruler).

Sages (Rishis): Vishvamitra (composed Gayatri Mantra, Mandala 3), Vasishtha (Sudas's Purohita, Mandala 7), Gritsamada (Mandala 2), Vamadeva (Mandala 4), Atri (Mandala 5), Bharadvaja (Mandala 6), Agastya (pioneer of Aryan culture southward).

topics.title: The Later Vedic Age (c. 1000 BC – 600 BC)
pointers: Sama Veda: Contains 1,875 verses (mostly drawn from the Rig Veda) set to musical melodies (Samans) for chanting during Soma sacrifices by the Udgatri priest; marks the origin of Indian classical music.
